analysis.one_liner: Restores expired limits on high earners' tax breaks and sends half the revenue to education.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring back two provisions of the tax code — the phaseout of personal exemptions and the limit on itemized deductions — that had been repealed by the 2001 tax cuts, raising revenue mostly from higher-income taxpayers. Half of that new revenue would go into a new Education Trust Fund for Department of Education programs, but only for programs whose funding rises above fiscal year 2005 levels, and only if Congress votes to appropriate the money each year. The other half of the revenue would stay in the Treasury with no designated purpose.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and families served by federally funded education programs, if Congress chooses to appropriate the new money and increase funding above 2005 levels. The bill would also slightly narrow a feature of the tax code that mainly benefits households with high incomes, many deductions, or large families — whose other taxpayers would effectively shoulder less of the federal burden as a result.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federally funded education programs and students

how_it_helps.text: Restores the personal exemption phaseout and the overall limit on itemized deductions, provisions the 2001 tax law had repealed, which raise revenue primarily from higher-income taxpayers.
Creates an Education Trust Fund and directs 50 percent of the new revenue into it, dedicated to Department of Education programs.
Trust fund money can only be spent on programs whose funding is increased above fiscal year 2005 levels, so it is designed to add to education budgets rather than replace existing money.

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income taxpayers. The personal exemption phaseout and the itemized deduction limit apply to taxpayers with larger incomes, more exemptions, or substantial itemized deductions, so restoring them would raise these households' federal tax bills beginning in tax year 2006.

drawbacks.text: Only half the new revenue is dedicated to education; the other half flows into the Treasury with no designated use, so the bill's headline education promise covers just a portion of what it raises.

The education money is not automatic: it can only be spent through annual appropriations bills, and only to the extent funding exceeds fiscal year 2005 levels, so Congress could decline to appropriate it and no new education spending would occur.

The restored phaseouts would raise taxes on many upper-middle-income households, not only the very wealthy — families with several children and homeowners with large deductions were among those affected by these provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward trade: higher taxes on households that pay most of the personal exemptions and itemized deductions at stake, in exchange for dedicated education funding. Its main weaknesses are design ones — only half the money is actually reserved for education, and even that half depends on future Congresses voting to appropriate it above a fixed 2005 baseline, which the bill cannot itself guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again — no hearing, no vote, and the Congress ended with it still sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on March 11, 2005, with Senator Richard Durbin as cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the committee never acted on it, and the full Senate never considered it.
That was the final action of record: the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 with the bill still in committee and no vote ever taken in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Higher-income taxpayers came out ahead: the exemption phaseout and deduction limit stayed repealed through the end of the decade as scheduled under the 2001 tax law, and no dedicated education funding stream was created. Public education programs gained nothing, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled its calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which he controlled as leader.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; the bill had two Democratic sponsors and sat in a Republican-led committee that took no action.

industries.note: Restoring the exemption phaseout and the itemized deduction limit would directly raise these households' federal tax bills starting in 2006. The revenue at stake was theirs to keep under the 2001 tax law's schedule, and the bill died, so they kept it.

industries.industry: Federally funded education programs (K-12 and Department of Education programs)
industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated funding stream for Department of Education programs, but only for spending above 2005 levels and only through annual appropriations — and the bill never advanced, so no money ever flowed.
